lesson.title: The Small Yes That Opens the Door to a Bigger One
lesson.summary: A persuasion strategy in which getting someone to agree to a small initial request makes them significantly more likely to agree to a larger, related request later.
lesson.body:
Salespeople, canvassers, and fundraisers have long known a trick that social psychologists eventually confirmed in the lab: if you want someone to agree to something big, it often helps to first get them to agree to something small. This is the foot-in-the-door technique, one of the best documented tools of persuasion. Rather than making the real request right away, the persuader opens with a modest request that almost anyone would accept, and only later follows up with the actual, larger request.

The classic demonstration comes from a 1966 study by Jonathan Freedman and Scott Fraser. Researchers posing as volunteers approached homeowners in a California neighborhood, and some were first asked to agree to a small, low effort request related to safe driving. A couple of weeks later, a different researcher visited the same homes and asked for something far more burdensome: permission to install a large, poorly lettered Drive Carefully sign on the front lawn. Homeowners who had already agreed to the small initial request were far more likely to agree to the large one than homeowners who were approached cold with only the big request, a difference the researchers described as large and consistent across several variations of the study.

Why does a tiny, seemingly unrelated first step change someone's willingness to make a large sacrifice later? The leading explanation draws on self-perception theory, the idea that people often figure out their own attitudes by observing their own behavior, especially when the reason for that behavior is not obvious. Someone who freely agrees to a small request with no reward or pressure to do so may start to think of themselves as the kind of person who supports that cause, a helpful neighbor, a safety conscious citizen. Once that self-image forms, agreeing to the bigger request that fits the same identity feels consistent rather than costly. This is a persuasion effect that works through the target's own mind rather than through argument or authority, which is what makes it worth studying alongside other persuasion techniques.

The technique has real limits. It tends to work best when the initial request is freely chosen rather than coerced or paid for, since a reward undercuts the self-perception effect. If you were paid to make the small commitment, you cannot conclude you did it out of genuine concern. It also seems to work better when some time separates the two requests and when both requests connect to a similar cause or identity. Outside the lab, the same logic shows up in employee training programs that start with small commitments, in habit forming apps that ask for tiny first actions, and in campaigns that start with low effort actions like sharing a post before asking for a donation or a knock on doors.
